name: Ohio
summary_text: Ohio is a state within the United States, so a visitor stands first under the national framework: Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to correct the application of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.  Entry screening carries an outing risk that applies at every United States port of entry, including Ohio's airports. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating an applicant who lists a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent fraud-based ban. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, and several foreign governments, including at least eight European states, adjusted travel guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.  Ohio's principal own measure concerns facilities. Governor Mike DeWine signed Senate Bill 104, the Protect All Students Act, on 27 November 2024; it took effect on 25 February 2025, ninety days after signing. The statute requires every public and private K-12 school, college and university in Ohio to designate restrooms, locker rooms, changing and shower rooms and overnight accommodations for the exclusive use of males or females on the basis of sex assigned at or near birth, which in practice directs trans students to facilities matching their birth-certificate sex.  The Ohio statute contains no enforcement mechanism. It was signed out of public view and over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil-rights groups, and was sponsored by Republican state Senator Jerry Cirino.  A national legal risk assessment published 27 August 2026 places Ohio in its worst-graded group of fifteen states, a tier below the four states flagged Do Not Travel (Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas), under a national frame of worst policies in effect.  Wider national exposure remains relevant to a visitor who is detained or needs care. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as chemical and surgical mutilation of children, some hospitals paused care, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

sources.title: Ray v. McCloud
sources.documents: Federal ruling invalidating Ohio's ban on amending gender marker on birth certificates as unconstitutional
sources.detail: Decided December 2020 by federal judge Michael H. Watson; Ohio Department of Health did not appeal; effective June 1, 2021 transgender individuals allowed to update birth certificate; filed March 2018 by four transgender Ohioans with ACLU and Lambda Legal support

sources.documents: Held discrimination on basis of transgender status is discrimination on basis of 'sex' under Title VII; employers may not use Religious Freedom Restoration Act to justify anti-LGBTQ discrimination
sources.detail: Covers Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Tennessee; case of Aimee Stephens, transgender woman fired in 2013 after disclosing transition at funeral home; appealed as R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes Inc. v. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission

name: Oklahoma
summary_text: Oklahoma is a state within the United States, so a visitor stands under the federal framework first. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and a civil-liberties union has sued the department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. By March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.  Entry screening carries a second exposure. The State Department announced on 25 February 2025 that it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth; the announcement followed an executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" issued on 5 February 2025. Separately, Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.  State facilities rules are where Oklahoma itself appears in the national picture. The Movement Advancement Project's national tracker, in its 25 March 2026 edition, lists Oklahoma under bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, specifically covering K-12 school facilities, with enactments in 2022 and again in 2025. Nationally, school and government-building bans of this kind apply in 9 states and 1 territory, and some states make trans use of facilities a criminal offence in certain circumstances, while 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law, and civil-rights attorneys described it as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.  Identity documents are the active legislative front in Oklahoma. On 6 May 2026 House Bill 1225, requiring a male or female designation on Oklahoma birth certificates and prohibiting changes with very little exception, passed its most recent vote 70-17 and headed to Governor Kevin Stitt's desk. Its authors said the bill is designed to strengthen the existing law being challenged in federal court by transgender plaintiffs including Tulsa resident Rowan Fowler, and the state Attorney General's office confirmed that the bill clarifies Oklahoma never permitted gender birth-certificate changes; critics called it further discrimination. The bill was still pending the governor's signature when last reported. Comparable closure is documented elsewhere: Kansas enacted a law in March 2026 invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, which rights groups call a template for other state legislatures.  Care for trans people is restricted federally and applies in Oklahoma. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as mutilation and some hospitals paused care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, proposed health-department rules in October 2025 would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, and in July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.  Custody and enforcement machinery round out the federal layer. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates mandating short hair, withdrawal of hormone medication and substitution of psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement, with severe sexual abuse also widely reported. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups, and a May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.  Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.

sources.title: Governor Stitt Executive Order - Definition of legal sex (August 2023)
sources.documents: Explicitly defines male and female as biological sexes assigned at birth for all state and legal purposes, including bathrooms/changing rooms in state facilities, sports, domestic violence shelters, rape crisis centers, incarceration, and statistics collection.
sources.detail: No URL in excerpt; cited as signed August 2023 by Gov. Kevin Stitt
